prompt.en: You log a contact at 0040 UTC on 8 March. The stated local offset is UTC minus 3 hours. Which local reminder matches the UTC entry?

explanation.en: Subtract three hours: the local clock reads 2140 on the previous date, 7 March. Adding moves in the wrong direction. Keeping 8 March with 2140 misses the date change; changing only the date leaves the clock wrong. Keep the original UTC date and time together in the log.

prompt.en: A club gives you an azimuthal map centred on its station, far from yours. Can you use its printed bearings directly to aim your home antenna?

text.en: Yes. Bearings depend only on the destination.
Yes, if you use the same UTC time as the club.
No. You need bearings from a map centred on your own location.
No. Azimuthal maps cannot show antenna bearings.

explanation.en: A bearing has a starting point as well as a destination. A different map centre can change the direction to aim. Sharing a time standard does not change map geometry; a correctly centred azimuthal map does show useful bearings.

prompt.en: A confirmation lists the right call sign but a different band from your log. What is the useful next step?

text.en: Compare UTC date, time, band, and mode with the other operator before accepting a match.
Accept it because a matching call sign proves every other field is correct.
Change your log to the confirmation details without checking.
Discard the log because Canadian amateurs do not have to keep one.

explanation.en: A call sign alone does not identify a particular contact. Compare the contact details and resolve the mismatch rather than overwriting evidence. Optional logs can still help match confirmations and find recording errors.
